name: full
_comment: The campaign that decides whether the fork is done. ~7 GiB dataset on an
11 GiB box, capped by cgroup so the working set is several times the
memory the engine is allowed and the OS page cache cannot hide the
difference. Budget is the engine's share of that cap: stock spends it all
on pages, BF splits it between pages and records at bf_page_cache_floor
-- which page_cache_floor now sweeps instead of assuming.
Write-heavy experiments run 30s instead of 20s (and warm up 8s): at
20s x 3 every one of them produced cells with >15% run-to-run spread.
A longer window straddles more WAL-checkpoint cycles, which is where
that variance came from; repeats went 3 -> 5 for every experiment.
Expect roughly 4-5 h including the one-time dataset load. Read-only
experiments reuse the database copy; write experiments each start from a
fresh copy of the pristine template (~10 s each).
Each experiment maps to a specific claim:
point_read     paper's 2x point-read win, at four cache sizes
page_cache_floor  how BF should split its budget between pages/records
skew           does the win depend on skew? (paper sweeps this)
scan           paper's 2.5x scan win, at three scan lengths
negative_read  phantom caching (paper 5.6)
update/insert  paper's 6x write win
workload_mix   the read/update sweep the paper reports
ycsb_*         standard mixes, so the numbers are comparable outside
durability_*   OUR addition: the record-WAL trade-off across
synchronous levels and group-commit sizes
write_amp      bytes on disk per commit, autocheckpoint off
overhead       bf_off vs stock: cost of the fork with the feature off

experiments.name: point_read
_why: memmax is "auto" (2x budget + 256M) rather than a fixed 1G. Under a
fixed cap the 512M budget owned half the cgroup and squeezed out the
OS page cache, so BOTH SUTs got slower as the budget grew -- the
2026-08-25 table falls from ~28k ops/s at 64M to ~21k at 512M. That
is a cgroup effect, not a cache-size effect, and it confounds the
axis. Scaling the cap keeps the engine at a constant fraction of
available memory so the axis varies cache size and nothing else.

experiments.name: page_cache_floor
_why: The axis that could not be measured before the bf_cache.c page-hash
fix. BF's pcache2 hash was pinned at 256 buckets for the life of the
cache, so a BF build with a real page cache walked ~nMax/256-long
chains and ran ~13x slower than pcache1 (measured: 43k vs 486k ops/s
at a 256M page cache). Every BF run was therefore held at the 8M
floor, which meant "equal memory budget" really compared stock's
tuned page cache against BF's record cache backed by almost no page
cache. Now the split itself is a variable.
stock ignores the floor and spends the whole budget on pages, so its
four rows are four independent measurements of one configuration --
a free estimate of the noise floor.

experiments.name: record_size
_why: Write-back insert refuses records above roughly 64-96 bytes and falls
back to the base-page path, so the write win is size-dependent. The
old wal_write_amp.sh used 64-byte payloads, i.e. exactly the size where
buffering always succeeds. This makes record size a measured axis
instead of a hidden assumption. Needs its own datasets: value_len is a
property of the loaded table, not of the run.
